title: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis
titleZh: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis
author: g-b-r
relevanceReason: 命中 2 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis Joint statement by the Lean and Mathlib communities, endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative. On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library comprising 17 million lines of code. We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement. Our rationale is outlined below. The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct. The four criteria in https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/ are all satisfied.
The statement of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct. This statement is part of Mathlib: RiemannHypothesis and has been carefully vetted by experts in Lean and number theory.

Alpöge’s library compiles correctly. By now, dozens of people have reported correct compilation of the codebase, reproducing the same raw proof export file. The library compiles without errors or build failures.

The code proves the correct statement. Crucially, the community has added a file that isolates the statement of the Riemann Hypothesis and imports only Mathlib. That statement was compared against the theorem proved by Alpöge using two independent tools (comparator and con-leche –compare), both confirming that the theorem proved in Alpöge’s library is exactly Mathlib’s statement of the Riemann Hypothesis.

The Lean proof is valid. The exported raw proof has been checked by several proof checkers, including Lean’s official kernel, the con-leche and con-ron checkers, and several independent checkers contributed by third parties and implemented in different programming languages. The checkers con-leche and con-ron come with a formal proof, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, thus addressing concerns that Lean’s logic itself might have flaws that the proof could exploit. An extensive overview is available at https://math.mit.edu/~drew/grh/. These checks ran on an inert export of the proof, out of reach of hypothetical malicious code in the Lean proof sources.

comments.author: rcr-anti
comments.textRawHtml: While still possible, the proof exploiting a bug is vanishingly small now. Following a few bugs and bad proofs this year, there are a number of different implementations, in different languages, and with different levels of proofs of their consistency. con-leche and con-ron are the heavy hitters, with consistency proofs of themselves. So for RH to be false, there'd have to be a bug in all the kernels that affects both the consistency proofs and the RH proof itself.

children.author: fspeech
children.textRawHtml: Also these AI proofs aren't exactly unreadable. There are many well known results embedded, which account for the bulk of the Lean code that you could ignore if you are comfortable with the well accepted theories. Then there is the high order AI construction. You may not understand how AI came up with it, like Ramanujan, but you could appreciate that it could have the properties claimed for it. You may even be able to check some for yourself. I don't know the high theories, but I do know that, for example at a few points, Anthropic model stuffed polynomials with hundreds of terms into proofs, like https://github.com/anthropics/fermats-last-theorem/blob/main... Out of sheer annoyance at how large the compiled olean files are and how long it takes my puny laptop to elaborate them, I asked the flash model I use to use sympy to factor and reduce and it didn't take much effort to get them to a more reasonable size. Of course these are trivial exercises but the point is to not be intimidated. If you do understand high theories you could fire up your favorite model and try to build a theory that we mere mortals could actually follow, at least in principle.

children.author: jychang
children.textRawHtml:
Correct.

They don't use some random definition of RiemannHypothesis, they use the version here: https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib...

Note that this definition is years old. It's very well vetted. It's not a case of "the proof works, it just doesn't actually prove what you think it proves".

If you read the blog post, it says they added a "Challenge.lean" file. What that means is that instead of taking for granted the proof is trying to prove Riemann, they added a small file which reads RiemannHypothesis from the Mathlib library mentioned above, and forces the proof to match that.

They also mention running comparator, which is important because it checks for all the ways a proof might mathematically "cheat". For example, if you are trying to prove 1+2=5, and you redefine 2 as 4, then your bad proof would actually compile in Lean at first, but then comparator checks would discover all the tricks like that and declare the proof invalid.

Additionally, they mention compiling the proof with different Lean kernels, not just the mainline one. This rules out a way a proof This means the proof cannot just take advantage of a bug in the mainline Lean kernel. Importantly, they mention compiling the proof with con-leche, which uses a kernel that has been mathematically verified. Using con-leche is a lot slower, but the fact that the proof works on multiple kernels including con-leche means that it's not taking advantage of some bug in Lean.

At this point, I would say the proof is almost certainly true. The only obvious way it could be false is if ZFC itself is inconsistent or something wild like that, and the proof took advantage of it. But if ZFC is inconsistent, all of mathematics is in trouble.

children.author: btilly
children.textRawHtml:
Yes, Lean is stronger than ZFC. But two of the checkers, con=leche and con-ron, don't just verify based on Lean. They come with a formal proof from set theory that they cannot wind up accepting an incorrect proof.

In other words you can ignore Lean. We have a proof from ZFC, of the Riemann Hypothesis. We have a proof, acceptable in ZFC, that this proof is correct.

In other words Lean's dependent type theory is used to arrange its understanding of the proof. But the actual reasoning that you wind up with for this proof does not need anything that doesn't follow from ZFC.

children.author: meowface
children.textRawHtml:
I wonder if in N years, when we (might) have crazy ASIs that make Fable 5.2 look like a nematode, maybe we'll see things like this as completely trivial and banal.

A machine intelligence might devise something as (seemingly) difficult as the Riemann hypothesis, but checking if what it posits is correct might be like a fast test command in a git repo, and so it can keep iterating on many ideas without being bottlenecked by waiting centuries or, perhaps even hours, to know if the ideas are true.

But then one could even imagine they'll one day be so powerful they could do this and more without ever using a formal system. They will just naturally be that comprehensive and rigorous internally, with something like Lean making them 100% instead of 99.99..% confident.

And eventually this would extend to almost everything, besides maybe biology where it may only be able to compress a human century into a day rather than into a second.

children.author: axmebhe
children.textRawHtml:
Mathematics could stall in some ways if the AIs continue to use brute force to prove these. Normally a mathematician would invent powerful new frameworks to solve a difficult problem (like Newton and calculus - there are many recent examples, as well).

As an outsider to the field, the strongest motivation for top mathematicians seems to be pride. I think the educational pipeline for top-level math will weaken if AIs are getting the credit for mathematical work.

children.author: mrandish
children.textRawHtml:
> become smart as the AIs

Treating "intelligence" as a single trait that can be cranked up like an RPG stat bar is a category error built on an ill-defined term.

"Intelligence" is a broad umbrella label for a variety of different capabilities: working memory, pattern matching, sensory integration, long-term recall, and domain-specific knowledge. LLMs running on designed digital silicon are fundamentally different from human minds running on evolved analog biology. They operate on separate substrates with divergent architectures, trade-offs, constraints and failure modes.

LLMs are fantastically useful tools that already beat humans at specific tasks. We built them to simulate specific human intellectual output we find valuable, but they do so using mechanisms which have almost nothing in common with how a brain works. Scaling up the simulation to increase the number and depth of tasks doesn't mean the underlying process is on a path to fully replace human cognition and reasoning.

children.author: LoganDark
children.textRawHtml:
I think it's because you no longer need to release knowledge if everyone can re-derive it independently. Work and learning lose its value when anyone can reproduce it without you, and when they can do it more trivially even than searching for your version. We're starting to reach the point where certain types of projects are just pointless now, because anyone who wants it can make their own version even better tailored to themselves. This isn't absolutely true of course, but the general discourse is heading in this direction, and this is one central focus of many modern imposter syndromes.

So everyone left without these tools to themselves is left in the dust. There are no more publishings of the most advanced knowledge and learnings, because everyone is expected to re-derive it from the prerequisites. But there's so much to derive that you just can't do it all on your own. It's not as natural and effortless as a large language model working through the course of whatever may require the knowledge and deriving it all in a depth first manner.

children.author: mcherm
children.textRawHtml:
I am not certain which "last time" you are thinking of, but I suspect that the answer IS the Lean verification.

If an AI writes a paper with an argument that X is true, it might be that X is true, or it might be that the argument in the paper is subtly flawed and X isn't true

On the other hand, if an AI generates a step-by-step proof in which each step can be mechanically verified, then people might have problems understanding the underlying ideas, but once it has been verified we know it won't have subtle errors. And that is basically what Lean is.

In this case, they not only have a Lean proof, they've verified it with more than one verification tool (so it's unlikely to be a bug in the verification tool) and double-checked whether the thing being proved really is what we intended to prove. That's rock solid.

Getting an UNDERSTANDING of the proof is another challenge, but at this point we can be quite certain it doesn't have errors.
